title: India's Generic Ozempic Revolution Hits a Wall as Dr. Reddy's Halts Semaglutide Production
excerpt: The supply disruption could delay affordable access to semaglutide for millions in India and Canada until late October — a setback for NRIs who had been counting on cheaper alternatives to manage diabetes and weight.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Dr. Reddy's halts semaglutide production due to quality issues, impacting supply in India and Canada.
  • Market reaction saw Dr. Reddy's lose approximately $678 million in market capitalization.
  • The delay in supply could last until late October 2026, affecting millions relying on affordable medication.
  • Alternative generic options remain available in India, but Canada faces a supply vacuum.
  • South Asians have high rates of diabetes and obesity, making affordable medication crucial.

India's generic pharmaceutical revolution in weight-loss and diabetes drugs has run into its first major roadblock. Dr. Reddy's Laboratories, one of India's largest generic drugmakers, has halted production of its semaglutide — the active ingredient in Novo Nordisk's blockbuster drugs Ozempic and Wegovy — after discovering that certain batches of the active pharmaceutical ingredient were "out of specification." The announcement sent shockwaves through markets on Thursday, wiping roughly $678 million from Dr. Reddy's market capitalisation in a single session. But for the millions of patients in India and the diaspora who had been eagerly awaiting affordable semaglutide, the real cost is time. ## What Happened During validation of a production scale-up, Dr. Reddy's identified a quality issue with its semaglutide API. CEO Erez Israeli told analysts that supplies would remain unavailable in India and face disruptions in Canada — where the company had launched its generic semaglutide earlier this year — until at least late October 2026. The company had originally targeted selling 12 million injectable pens in its first year. That ambition has now been cut nearly in half: Israeli said the company is on track to supply six to seven million pens in the second half of the year, but acknowledged the earlier July-to-September window is essentially lost. "When we gave the earlier target we assumed we would sell between July to September. Now unlikely we will do that," Israeli said on the analyst call. > **""When we gave the earlier target we assumed we would sell between July to September."** The ripple effects are already spreading. Torrent Pharmaceuticals has recalled selected batches of its own Semalix injection pens for technical evaluation after a notification from Dr. Reddy's, raising questions about shared API supply chains across India's generic ecosystem. ## Why This Matters for the Diaspora The semaglutide patent expiry in India on March 20, 2026 was celebrated as a watershed moment. Within weeks, over 40 Indian generic manufacturers had launched their own versions at prices starting from ₹1,290 per month — a fraction of Ozempic's original ₹8,800-11,000 monthly cost. For NRIs, the implications ran in two directions. Those managing diabetes or obesity in India suddenly had access to dramatically cheaper medication. And in Canada, where Dr. Reddy's had begun selling its generic version, Indo-Canadian patients were among the earliest adopters. The disruption now creates a supply vacuum in both markets. Patients currently on Dr. Reddy's semaglutide in Canada face the prospect of switching brands mid-treatment — not medically dangerous, but disruptive to dosing schedules and doctor-patient management plans. In India, where dozens of generics compete, the impact is distributed: Sun Pharma, Cipla, Zydus, and Lupin continue to supply their own versions, so patients have alternatives. ## The Bigger Picture

South Asians face disproportionately high rates of type 2 diabetes and obesity-related cardiovascular disease. A 2026 study published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health documented how immigration stress, dietary shifts, and sedentary urban lifestyles compound these metabolic risks for the diaspora. India already has more than 77 million people living with type 2 diabetes and one of the world's largest populations of overweight adults. The generic semaglutide wave was seen as a public health accelerator — making GLP-1 receptor agonists accessible to the masses, not just the affluent. Dr. Reddy's has stressed that there is "no impact on patient safety or on the product's existing global regulatory filings." The issue is purely about future supply, not the safety of pens already distributed. But for a market that was counting on rapid scaling, even a three-month delay matters. ## What Patients Should Know If you are currently using a Dr. Reddy's semaglutide product in India or Canada, consult your prescribing physician about alternatives. Multiple generic semaglutide brands remain available in India, including Sun Pharma's Sematrinity, Cipla's offering, Alkem's Semasize, and Natco Pharma's vials. In Canada, options may be more limited; your doctor can advise on switching to another brand or temporarily adjusting your treatment plan. Dr. Reddy's says it expects to resume supplies by late October, but has not given a specific restart date. The company's next quarterly earnings call will likely provide an update on the API remediation timeline. *Sources: Reuters, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories analyst call (July 9, 2026), MedicalXpress, Forbes India, Livemint*
